strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: adapting web agents to new environments without human-annotated tasks/trajectories or test-set leakage, which is a genuine pain point in current web-agent literature.

The dual-refinement design (task refinement during trajectory collection + post-hoc trajectory refinement) is a sensible, clearly articulated extension of prior work (OS-Genesis, Explorer), and the paper does a good job explaining conceptually why underspecified initial tasks lead to noisy trajectories.

Reasonably thorough empirical protocol: consistent LLM (GPT-4.1) across all baselines and the proposed method for fair comparison, two different open-source backbone models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B), and a controlled, reproducible environment (WebArena with Docker) rather than a live website.

Multiple complementary analyses beyond headline accuracy: task diversity via t-SNE and quality scores, trajectory completion-rate breakdown (completed/failed/exceeded budget), API cost comparison, component-wise ablation (SS/CE/TR/JR), and data-scaling curves.
Illustrative case studies (Figures 5–6) make the refinement mechanism concrete and interpretable, aiding understanding of what the method actually does.
weaknesses: All data-quality and diversity metrics (Tables 2–3, t-SNE distances) are produced by GPT-4.1-as-judge, the very same model used to generate and refine the synthetic data. This creates a circularity/self-preference risk: the model may rate its own outputs and refinement style favorably, undermining the claimed "quality" gains as independent evidence; no human verification of task feasibility or trajectory correctness is reported.

Absolute success rates are low and, more importantly, internally inconsistent with the paper's own framing: SynthAgent's synthetic-data model (e.g., 20.80% for Qwen) sometimes exceeds the stated "upper bound" SFT model trained on real test-set tasks (16.37%), which is not adequately explained and calls into question either the upper-bound framing, evaluation protocol, or comparability of training set sizes/qualities.

Evaluation uses a reduced WebArena set (226/812 tasks, one per template) with small per-site counts (26–57), and no repeated runs, variance, or confidence intervals are reported for any table, making it hard to judge whether the reported gains (e.g., +5.1 avg over OS-Genesis) are statistically meaningful rather than noise, especially given per-site results are quite volatile (e.g., UI-TARS Shopping: Ours ties OS-Genesis at 20.00 vs 21.82).

The Explorer baseline's very poor, near-degenerate performance (4.44%/4.96%, 68.3% of trajectories exceeding budget) is surprising given it is a published, peer-reviewed method; since it was re-implemented by the authors rather than using original code/checkpoints, there is a risk the reimplementation disadvantages this comparator, which is central to the paper's contrastive narrative.

Method contribution is somewhat incremental — it is essentially the combination of ideas from OS-Genesis (categorized/triplet-based exploration) and Explorer (iterative task refinement) plus a new post-hoc trajectory-cleaning step, with limited theoretical grounding for the specific heuristics (the hallucination predicate C, the four conservative edit types) beyond intuitive design choices.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: code is promised ("will be publicly available") but not provided at submission, and reliance on a closed proprietary API (GPT-4.1) for all synthesis/refinement/judging steps limits exact reproducibility and independent verification by other researchers.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically relevant problem: adapting web agents to new, unseen website environments without costly human-collected demonstrations.

The dual-refinement idea (task refinement during trajectory collection + post-hoc global-context trajectory refinement) is a sensible design that is clearly motivated by concrete failure modes of prior work (hallucinated tasks, noisy/misaligned trajectories).

Reasonably thorough ablation study (Table 4) isolating the contribution of categorized exploration, task refinement, and trajectory refinement, showing each component adds value, and a useful analysis of why the Explorer baseline fails (task drift causing budget-exceeding trajectories).
Extensive appendix with full prompt templates for task categorization, task generation, task refinement, and trajectory refinement, which aids reproducibility of the pipeline.
Includes a data-scaling study and qualitative case studies (Figures 5–6) that make the mechanism of the method concrete and interpretable.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains low across the board (e.g., 20.8% and 17.3% overall success rate for the two backbones), well below the SFT upper bound and sometimes close to or below the zero-shot GPT-4.1 numbers; the practical significance of the reported gains is unclear.

All data-quality metrics (task/trajectory quality, diversity) as well as the trajectory-completion judgments in Tables 2–3 are produced by the same GPT-4.1 model that is also used for data synthesis and refinement, creating a self-evaluation / self-preference confound with no human validation of these scores.

Evaluation is conducted on only 226 WebArena tasks (one run per task, no repeated trials, no variance/confidence intervals reported), which is a noisy basis given binary task success and known stochasticity of LLM-based agents; many reported deltas between methods (e.g., a few percentage points per website) could plausibly fall within noise.

The Explorer baseline's extremely poor performance (often below the untrained base model, with 68.3% of trajectories exceeding the step budget) is surprising for a published, competitive method; the reimplementation details are thin, raising concerns about whether the comparison is fully fair and whether Explorer was tuned/adapted appropriately for WebArena's authenticated, complex sites.
Single testbed (WebArena only) limits generalizability of the claimed improvements to other web environments or realistic live websites.

The method's novelty is somewhat incremental: it mainly combines/engineers existing ideas (OS-Genesis-style exploration, Explorer-style task refinement, LLM-based trajectory editing) with heuristic triggers (ExistsUI, MissingArgs, Stall) rather than introducing a fundamentally new technique, and the 'fully synthetic, human-free' framing undersells the substantial reliance on a strong proprietary LLM (GPT-4.1) for every stage, which affects cost and reproducibility for practitioners without such access.

Code is only promised ('will be publicly available') and not yet released, and key implementation details (e.g., exact hyperparameters for stall/args detection, exact categorization heuristics beyond examples) are only partially specified, which could hinder faithful reproduction.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: adapting web agents to new environments via fully synthetic supervision, with a clear articulation of the specific failure modes (task hallucination, trajectory noise) that motivate the method.

The dual-refinement design (task refinement during collection + post-hoc trajectory refinement) is a sensible and clearly explained combination of ideas, and the paper provides a systematic ablation (Table 4) that isolates the contribution of categorized exploration, task refinement, and trajectory refinement, showing each component matters and that trajectory refinement is necessary to realize the benefit of task refinement.

Comparisons against multiple relevant and reasonably strong baselines (Self-Instruct, OS-Genesis, Explorer) across two different open-source backbone agents (Qwen2.5-VL, UI-TARS) and five WebArena websites give a fairly comprehensive empirical picture.

Additional diagnostic analyses (t-SNE task diversity, trajectory completion/exceed rates, cost comparison, data scaling curve) go beyond simple end-task accuracy and help explain why SynthAgent outperforms Explorer/OS-Genesis (e.g., Explorer's frequent goal changes lead to 68.3% of trajectories exceeding the step budget).

Use of WebArena (Dockerized, controllable) supports reproducibility of the evaluation environment, and the appendix provides full prompts for every refinement/generation stage, aiding replication of the pipeline.
weaknesses: Nearly all fine-grained quality metrics (task quality, task diversity, trajectory quality/completion rates in Tables 2-3) are scored by GPT-4.1, the same model used for task/trajectory generation and refinement in SynthAgent. This creates a circularity/self-evaluation bias that is not discussed or mitigated (e.g., via a second independent judge model or human validation), weakening confidence in these auxiliary claims even though the downstream fine-tuning results offer a more independent check.

Absolute downstream performance remains low and leaves a substantial gap to the SFT (test-task) upper bound, particularly for UI-TARS (17.26% vs 23.45%), and even the fine-tuned models often underperform zero-shot GPT-4.1 (25.22%). This tempers the practical impact of the proposed adaptation despite the relative gains over other synthetic baselines.

The evaluation set is small (226 tasks total, e.g., only 26 for Reddit), and no variance/significance analysis (multiple seeds, confidence intervals) is reported, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (often a few points) are statistically robust, especially given some tied/coincidental values across methods (e.g., identical Shopping scores for +Self-Instruct/+Ours on UI-TARS).

The Explorer baseline underperforms even the un-adapted base model by a wide margin, which is explained qualitatively (authentication issues, frequent task drift) but not otherwise validated; since this is a reimplementation with different backbone LLM (GPT-4.1) than the original paper, there is a risk that baseline underperformance is partly an artifact of reimplementation choices rather than intrinsic to the method, and no sanity check against reported Explorer numbers is provided.

Evaluation is confined to a single benchmark family (WebArena's five fixed simulated websites), so claims about "adapting to new environments" are not tested on genuinely diverse or real-world websites; external validity beyond this controlled testbed is unverified.

Several implementation choices (context window of 3, up to 2 sampled elements per category, 500 task-trajectory pairs per site) are stated as empirically set without ablation, leaving their sensitivity/robustness unexamined.

The framing of "without human involvement" slightly overstates the contribution, since the method depends on carefully hand-engineered refinement predicates (ExistsUI, MissingArgs, Stall) and multiple detailed prompts crafted by the authors; the novelty is more in combining/refining existing synthetic-data ideas than introducing fundamentally new techniques.

strengths: Clearly identifies and motivates two concrete failure modes in prior synthetic web-agent data pipelines (task hallucination and trajectory noise), framing them as a coherent design tension between environment grounding and execution noise.

The proposed dual refinement (conflict-triggered task refinement during execution + post-hoc global trajectory refinement) and categorized exploration are sensible, well-motivated design choices, and the paper provides detailed qualitative case studies (Figures 5-6) illustrating how each component behaves.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation: results on both a controlled benchmark (WebArena, 5 websites) and a more realistic large-scale benchmark (Online-Mind2Web, 136 websites), with two different open-source backbone agents (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B).
Thorough ablations (categorized exploration, task refinement, trajectory refinement) and a data-scaling study that support the claimed contribution of each component.

Quality/diversity metrics are cross-validated with three different LLM judges (GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, Qwen3-30B), showing consistent relative rankings across baselines, which somewhat strengthens confidence in the comparative claims.
Detailed appendix with prompts, implementation details, and statistics that aid reproducibility of the pipeline (though full code release is not verifiable from the manuscript).
weaknesses: A central soundness concern: the paper frames SFT-on-test-tasks as an 'upper bound,' yet for the Qwen backbone SynthAgent (20.80 overall) actually outperforms this supposed upper bound (16.37), which is not adequately explained and raises questions about the reliability/comparability of the main WebArena results.

Evaluation set for WebArena is small (226 tasks, one run per condition apparently), and no variance, multiple seeds, or significance testing is reported anywhere in the paper, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (e.g., +5.1 over OS-Genesis) are robust to noise inherent in LLM-based generation/evaluation and stochastic agent rollouts.

Quality/diversity metrics rely entirely on LLM-as-judge scoring, and the same GPT-4.1 model used to synthesize/refine SynthAgent's data is also used as one of the primary judges, creating potential circularity that could bias quality/diversity comparisons in the method's favor; no human evaluation is included to validate these automatic scores.

The Explorer baseline's very poor performance (near-zero success rate on several websites, 68.3% budget overruns) seems disproportionately weak relative to its reported performance in its original paper; while the authors attempt to justify this via re-implementation details, the magnitude of degradation (sometimes below the untrained base model) raises concern about whether the re-implementation is fully faithful/fair, which is important since Explorer is one of the two main points of comparison.

The diversity metric (a single scalar score per method, with t-SNE visualization) is only loosely described, without clear methodology for how the numeric diversity score is computed from embeddings, limiting reproducibility of this specific analysis.
Absolute success rates remain low across the board (roughly 15-30%), and the practical significance/impact of the reported gains for real-world deployment is not deeply discussed.

The code repository link is not filled in in the abstract, and while this may be for anonymity, it leaves reproducibility of the full pipeline (which involves many LLM-prompted stages) unverifiable at review time.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and reasonable design tension (task grounding vs. trajectory noise) and proposes a coherent four-stage pipeline (categorized exploration, conflict-triggered task refinement, global trajectory refinement, fine-tuning) that directly targets this tension.

Ablation studies (Table 5) and trajectory-completion statistics (Table 4) do provide some component-level evidence that each proposed stage (categorized exploration, task refinement, trajectory refinement) contributes to the final performance.

Evaluation spans two different benchmark settings (offline WebArena and online Mind2Web across 136 live sites), which is a reasonable attempt to test generalization beyond a single controlled environment.
The paper includes fairly extensive implementation details and prompts in the appendix, which aids understanding of the pipeline mechanics.
weaknesses: Severe evaluation circularity: nearly all quality/diversity metrics (Table 3, 10, 11, and the diversity scores used for the t-SNE narrative) are produced by LLM judges from the same model family (GPT-4.1/GPT-5.1) that also generated and refined the data. Since SynthAgent's refinement stages are themselves driven by the identical LLM, the 'quality' improvements it reports are largely self-referential and do not constitute independent validation; no human evaluation of task feasibility, hallucination rates, or trajectory correctness is reported anywhere in the paper.

Test sets per website are very small (26–57 tasks for WebArena sub-splits), and the paper reports single-run point estimates with no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results despite the inherent stochasticity of LLM-based generation, refinement, and agent execution. Several reported gains between methods are only a few percentage points, which is difficult to trust as significant given this sample size and lack of repeated trials.

The Explorer baseline reimplementation performs implausibly poorly, even degrading below the untrained base model (e.g., 4.44 vs. 8.80 for Qwen), which is a suspicious result for a peer-reviewed prior method; the authors themselves note they added authentication support that the original method lacked, raising concern that implementation choices specific to the reimplementation (rather than the algorithmic design per se) may be inflating the apparent superiority of SynthAgent. No other closely related baselines mentioned in Section 2.3 (e.g., Learn-by-Interact, NNetNav, WebSynthesis, AgentTrek) are empirically compared, despite being called directly relevant.

The paper's own 'upper bound' (SFT on actual test-set tasks) is inconsistently positioned: SynthAgent's fully synthetic data outperforms the test-task SFT upper bound on Qwen overall (20.80 vs. 16.37) without any explanation of why training on unrelated synthetic tasks should exceed training on in-distribution test tasks; this undermines the framing of SFT as an informative upper bound and is not discussed or investigated.

Absolute performance remains low across the board (teens to twenties percent success rate), and in several cases the fine-tuned models with the proposed synthetic data still underperform the raw untrained GPT-4.1 agent (e.g., 20.80 vs. 25.22 overall), which tempers claims about the practical value of the adaptation approach.

The abstract's code availability statement is incomplete ('The code is publicly available at' with no URL), raising basic reproducibility concerns for a paper whose central claim rests on a complex, multi-stage LLM-driven synthetic data pipeline that would be very difficult to reproduce from the paper's description alone.

Judge disagreement across evaluators (Table 2) is substantial (e.g., SynthAgent scored 31.67 by GPT-4.1 vs. 15.67 by GPT-5.1), which is not discussed but signals high measurement noise in the online benchmark results, further weakening confidence in the reported superiority claims.

strengths: The paper identifies and clearly articulates a real, well-motivated design tension in existing synthetic web-agent data pipelines (task hallucination from single-step task proposal vs. trajectory noise from continuous online task refinement), and grounds this observation in concrete empirical comparisons with two closely related prior works (OS-Genesis, Explorer).

The proposed dual refinement approach (conflict-triggered task refinement during execution + post-hoc global-context trajectory refinement) is a sensible and reasonably novel resolution to the identified tension, and the paper provides a clear algorithmic description (conflict predicate, refinement principles, edit operation types).

Experiments are fairly extensive: two benchmarks (WebArena and the more realistic Online-Mind2Web), multiple LLM judges (GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, WebJudge/Qwen3-30B) for robustness of quality/diversity evaluation, two different open-source backbone agents (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B), and a data-scaling study.

Thorough ablation study isolating the contribution of categorized exploration, task refinement, and trajectory refinement individually and jointly, along with a specific investigation into why Explorer underperforms (refinement frequency, budget exceedance rate, API cost).

All baselines are re-implemented with the same underlying LLM (GPT-4.1) for fair comparison, and the paper documents implementation choices (e.g., adding authentication support to Explorer) transparently.
Useful qualitative case studies (Figures 5-6) and detailed appendix (prompts, category taxonomies, per-environment statistics) support reproducibility of the method's mechanics.
weaknesses: Nearly all quality/diversity metrics used to support the central 'higher quality synthetic data' claim (task quality, task diversity, trajectory quality) are LLM-as-judge scores rather than externally validated or human-verified metrics; since the same or closely related LLM family (GPT-4.1/GPT-5.1) is used both to generate/refine the data and to judge it, there is a risk of self-consistency bias inflating SynthAgent's advantage, and no human evaluation is reported to corroborate these automatic scores.

A notable inconsistency undermines the framing of the main WebArena result: the paper describes SFT on actual test-set tasks as 'an informative upper bound,' yet for Qwen2.5-VL, SynthAgent (20.80) clearly exceeds this claimed upper bound (16.37). This is not adequately explained beyond a general note about trajectory noise in the SFT baseline, and it raises questions about whether the SFT baseline was implemented/tuned as strongly as SynthAgent (e.g., same refinement quality control was not applied to its trajectories), complicating interpretation of the comparison.

Absolute task success rates remain low across the board (mostly under 30%, several methods under 20%), and fine-tuned 7B agents using SynthAgent's synthetic data still generally underperform the raw GPT-4.1 zero-shot baseline (25.22 overall vs. 20.80/17.26). This tempers the practical significance of the reported gains, though the relative comparison to other synthetic-data baselines remains informative.

Evaluation sets per website are small (26-57 tasks for WebArena subsets, ~100 per judge on Online-Mind2Web with only ~50 GPT-5.1 samples implied), and no variance/multiple-seed results or significance testing are reported, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains over OS-Genesis (the strongest baseline) are statistically robust rather than noise, especially in categories with small sample counts (e.g., Reddit n=26).

The method introduces numerous heuristic hyperparameters (conflict predicate thresholds such as '3 consecutive no-ops,' sampling '2 unvisited elements per category,' context window of 3 steps, step budget of 30) without sensitivity analysis, leaving unclear how robust performance is to these design choices.

No comparison to RL-based web agent training methods is provided, despite being discussed in related work as an alternative paradigm; this limits the scope of the empirical claims about the framework's overall competitiveness.

The code repository link is missing/empty in the submitted manuscript, and while prompts are given in the appendix, full reproducibility (exact hyperparameters for data collection pipelines, training configs beyond the brief mention, judge prompt calibration) depends on the promised code release, which cannot currently be verified.
